newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Foreign agencies leave Chechnya after murder.
newsitem.headline: Foreign agencies leave Chechnya after murder.

text.p: Most international aid agencies were pulling out of Russia's breakaway Chechnya region on Wednesday after gunmen shot six foreign aid workers there dead on Tuesday.

Russian officials, who are struggling to release policemen held hostage since Saturday by a Chechen field commander, vowed to track down the killers of five women and a man working for the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
The six were killed by masked gunmen as they were sleeping in a Red Cross hospital compound in the village of Novye Atagi.
They came from Norway, the Netherlands, Canada, Spain and New Zealand. A seventh worker, a Swiss who ran the project, was wounded.

"We have suspended our activities in Chechnya in solidarity with our ICRC colleagues," Aleth Jaurou from the North Caucasus mission of Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF) told Reuters in Nazran, capital of the Ingushetia region which borders Chechnya.
MSF workers were among the first to land in Chechnya after Russia sent troops there in December 1994 to quell the region's independence drive.
The fighting devastated the southern province and tens of thousands of people were killed in 21 months of fighting.
Jaurou could not say how long the suspension would last.

The ICRC said on Tuesday it was withdrawing all its international staff, leaving local staff to look after the Novye Atagi hospital and other Chechnya relief offices. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and Paris-based medical charity Medecins du Monde also scaled back their work.
Interfax news agency quoted Russia's Deputy Interior Minister Vladimir Kolesnikov as saying Russian police had stepped up efforts to investigate the murder.
"We have good reason to believe that in the near future it will become clear who committed this crime," he said in Moscow.
It was not clear how Russian police could investigate events in Chechnya. Most Russian troops have left the region under a controversial peace deal and the rebels control the region.
The separatist leaders have vowed to investigate the killings and to extradite the gunmen to the countries where the murdered workers came from.
But an incident on Saturday clearly showed the limits of their powers in Chechnya.
Fighters loyal to field commander Salman Raduyev seized 21 Russian policemen who tried to prevent them from entering the ethnic republic of Dagestan next to Chechnya.

Top separatist officials, who are keen to end the incident that could upset a fragile peace process and threaten local elections scheduled for January 27, have promised to force Raduyev to release all his hostages unconditionally.
But Raduyev said on Tuesday he wanted apologies from Russia for not letting him into Dagestan and could kill the hostages if anyone tried to free them by force.
Senior Kremlin official Boris Berezovsky is in Chechnya trying to speed up the release of the policemen.

In an unrelated incident reported by Interfax, authorities in another north Caucasus region, North Ossetia, said three senior officials had been kidnapped in Chechnya by gunmen seeking a $6 million ransom.
The kidnapping did not appear to be politically motivated.
Kidnappings for ransom have become frequent in Chechnya where armed groups which fought against Russia in the war are jobless after a peace deal struck on August 31.
